Modern.brandNameRationale: Aperture is the foundational camera term for the lens opening — single trade word, deeply specific to photography. Studio is the plain category suffix. Stands in the lineage of trade-vocabulary photography brands (Magnum, Aperture Foundation register).
Modern.industrySummary: Modern photography studios are competing on visual signature as much as on the client roster. Editorial, commercial, and brand photography has consolidated around studios with strong points of view. The mid-market is moving toward design-led practices.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Tom Sloan (tomsloan.co) holds the modern commercial peer position. Bobby Doherty (bobbydoherty.com) does the editorial-still-life corner. Petra Collins (petracollins.com) carries the lifestyle-fashion side. Maurizio Cattelan's collaborators set the conceptual top. We sit closer to Tom Sloan in posture, with a sharper brand surface.
Modern.positioningStatement: A commercial photography studio with one visual signature and a small client list.

targetAudience.primary: Art directors, brand managers, and creative directors at mid-size brands and editorial titles. They book the studio because the look fits the brief, not because the price is lowest.

dos: Show the work, then the credits
Name the photographer on every shoot
donts: Photograph the studio empty at golden hour

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. Aperture Studio in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, a thin rectangular frame outline, used as the watermark on every image, the favicon, and the email signature.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A site that loads the work, then the studio, then the contact. A printed monograph published every two years. A small studio open by appointment. A signature visual style that holds across every project.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Atelier is the French word for a craft workshop. Norden suggests a Northern European register: Scandinavian or Northern English, both associated with quiet craft. The pair reads as a small heritage studio that takes its time.
Luxury.story: Atelier Norden began with a single photographer who had spent decades inside larger studios and wanted to take fewer commissions, more carefully. The studio accepts a limited number of sittings each year. Some clients have been with the studio for two generations.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end portrait and family photography has been moving toward larger studios and faster turnarounds. There's a parallel market for small heritage studios in the older tradition. Few clients, long sittings, archival prints. The customer is paying for the photographer, the workshop, and the next sitting in a decade.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Annie Leibovitz's studio (annieleibovitz.com) holds the institutional peak. Mario Testino (mariotestino.com) sits in the celebrity-portrait tier. Karim Sadli (karimsadli.com) does the editorial-meets-portraiture middle. We sit smaller than all of them, in the heritage-portrait specialism.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small portrait studio for families and individuals who treat the sitting as a generational record.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy families. Heads of established institutions. People who treat the photograph as an heirloom. Often the sitting is for a milestone (wedding, birth, succession, retirement, death).

dos: Speak in the language of craft, not service

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn camera-aperture hallmark, three thin arcs forming a closed shape, used on archival print backings, the order book, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles the few digital surfaces. Both restrained.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Portrait is the most basic photography category: the photograph of a person. The brand puts the genre in the brand position, plain and unadorned.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most photography studios offer everything: weddings, portraits, commercial, lifestyle, product. There's an opening for one that does one thing only.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most studios fail this purity test. The closest spirit is some Japanese portrait practices and the early Avedon studio model: one genre, done very well.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A studio that takes portraits. That is the entire offering.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who want a portrait. They don't want a 'shoot'. They don't want lifestyle content. They want a still picture of themselves or someone they love, made by a person who knows how to make one.

dos: Confirm the sitting in one short message
donts: Sell prints separately from the sitting fee

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Standard signals industry-grade, reliable, on-spec. Image is the category. Group closes it as a B2B services firm. The whole name reads like a real, established production company already on the procurement panel at Fortune 500 marketing departments.
Corporate.industrySummary: Commercial photography and visual production is a B2B category dominated by either huge production companies (Wieden+Kennedy's in-house teams, Stink) or thousands of small studios. The opening is a mid-size production firm focused on enterprise marketing visual needs.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Smyle (smyle.com) handles the production side in Europe. Mishpacha (mishpacha.co) holds the corporate-photo middle. Trunk Archive (trunkarchive.com) is the photography licensing peer. We sit closer to Smyle in scope, more design-led.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Visual production services for enterprise marketing teams.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Enterprise marketing teams need production partners who can deliver photography, video, and visual content across campaigns at consistent quality, with the operational discipline of a procurement-ready vendor.

Creative.tagline: A photography studio that still prints.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Darkroom is the trade name for the film-development working room — single trade compound, archaic in the digital era. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school.
Creative.manifesto: Most photography brands sell soft light. The flattering portrait, the golden hour, the warm afternoon. We made Hard Light because the photographs that last are the ones with the shadow still in them. We sell the actual face, the actual moment, the actual color. We are not a flattering brand. We are not for every client. We are for the ones who want the real picture.
Creative.industrySummary: Photography branding has been soft, warm, and slightly twee. There's room for a studio that's sharp, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and still produces editorial-grade work.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Juergen Teller (juergenteller.com) holds the canonical hard-light editorial position. Wolfgang Tillmans (tillmans.co.uk) sits in the conceptual peer group. Pierre Debusschere (pdb.bz) does the contemporary hard-edge fashion. We sit younger and more brand-aware than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A photography studio for clients who want the real picture, not the flattering one.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 45. Art directors at editorial titles, creative directors at sharper-edged fashion brands, and the small set of musicians and designers who book photographers based on signature.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display sans, with the L of LIGHT cast in a thicker stroke to suggest harder light. Standalone hard-edge L icon for stickers, social profiles, and the back of every printed print.
